![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14251174/assets/698d7433fbee56d80815412425dfd2b761a618f364667f809ddc072762ad2b19.png)

Which of the following represents the area enclosed by the first petal of the polar curve 
 $r=2(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )),$
 represented by the shaded region shown above?
questions.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r(\theta )=2(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =2{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta \end{aligned}
$$

We now proceed to find the integration limits. 

The curve bounding the region crosses itself at the origin. Therefore, we want to find the values of $\theta $ for which $r=0$, or 

$$
\begin{aligned}2(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )) & =0 \\ 1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ) & =0 \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ) & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

From the diagram, the first petal extends from the fourth quadrant to the first quadrant. Since the petal begins in the fourth quadrant, it is convenient to allow negative values of $\theta $ when determining the interval.

The solutions for $2\theta $ closest to $0$ on either side are

$$
2\theta =-\pi ,\pi \,⟹\,\theta =-\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2}
$$

Therefore, the first petal is traversed for 

$$
\theta \in [-\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2}].
$$

 

Notice that this interval lies between the fourth and first quadrants, the same as our petal.

Therefore, our expression for the area is given by

$$
2{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Which of the following represents the area enclosed by the first petal of the polar curve  $r=1+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ),$ represented by the shaded region shown above?
questions.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r(\theta )=1+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{(1+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ))}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta \end{aligned}
$$

We now proceed to find the integration limits. 

The curve bounding the region crosses itself at the origin. Therefore, we want to find the values of $\theta $ for which $r=0$, or 

$$
\begin{aligned}1+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ) & =0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ) & =-\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

From the diagram, the first petal extends from the fourth quadrant to the second quadrant. Since the petal begins in the fourth quadrant, it is convenient to allow negative values of $\theta $ when determining the interval.

The solutions for $2\theta $ closest to $0$ on either side are

$$
2\theta =-\frac{\pi }{6},\frac{7\pi }{6}\,⟹\,\theta =-\frac{\pi }{12},\frac{7\pi }{12}
$$

Therefore, the first petal is traversed for 

$$
\theta \in [-\frac{\pi }{12},\frac{7\pi }{12}].
$$

 

Notice that this interval starts in the fourth quadrant and ends in the second quadrant, the same as our petal.

Therefore, our expression for the area is given by

$$
\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /12}^{7\pi /12}{(1+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ))}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Which of the following represents the area enclosed by the first petal of the polar curve
 $r=\sqrt{|\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta +\frac{\pi }{4})|},$
 represented by the shaded region shown above?
questions.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r(\theta )=\sqrt{|\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta +\frac{\pi }{4})|}$, we obtain

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}|\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta +\frac{\pi }{4})|\,\text{d}\theta 
$$

We now proceed to find the integration limits. 

The curve bounding the region crosses itself at the origin. Therefore, we want to find the values of $\theta $ for which $r=0$, or 

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta +\frac{\pi }{4}) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

From the diagram, the first petal extends from the fourth quadrant to the first quadrant. Since the petal begins in the fourth quadrant, it is convenient to allow negative values of $\theta $ when determining the interval.

The solutions for $2\theta +\frac{\pi }{4}$ closest to $0$ on either side are

$$
2\theta +\frac{\pi }{4}=-\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2}\,⟹\,2\theta =-\frac{3\pi }{4},\frac{\pi }{4}\,⟹\,\theta =-\frac{3\pi }{8},\frac{\pi }{8}.
$$

Therefore, the first petal is traversed for 

$$
\theta \in [-\frac{3\pi }{8},\frac{\pi }{8}].
$$

 

Notice that this interval lies between the fourth and first quadrants, the same as our petal.

Therefore, our expression for the area is given by

$$
\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-3\pi /8}^{\pi /8}|\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta +\frac{\pi }{4})|\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

questions.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r(\theta )=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(8\theta )$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{(2\operatorname{cos}⁡(8\theta ))}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{cos}^{2}⁡(8\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

We now proceed to find the integration limits. 

The curve bounding the region crosses itself at the origin. Therefore, we want to find the values of $\theta $ for which $r=0$, or 

$$
2\operatorname{cos}⁡(8\theta )=0.
$$

Notice that the first petal lies between the first and fourth quadrants. So it's convenient to assume that $\theta $ can be negative.

We now solve the above equation for $8\theta \in [-\pi ,\pi ):$

$$
8\theta =-\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2}\,⟹\,\theta =-\frac{\pi }{16},\frac{\pi }{16}
$$

Therefore, the first petal is traversed for $\theta \in [-\frac{\pi }{16},\frac{\pi }{16}].$ Notice that this interval lies between the first and fourth quadrants, the same as our petal.

Therefore, our expression for the area is given by

$$
2{\int }_{-\pi /16}^{\pi /16}{cos}^{2}⁡(8\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .
$$
